8.title: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
8.hook: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
8.carry: sit on the floor with a stranger
8.howItsDone: Gurdwaras run a langar: volunteers cook a simple vegetarian meal and serve it free to anyone, traditionally seated together in rows on the floor.

segments.voice: Last week ended with simran, remembrance. Your line was remember on the inhale. Did a red light or a kettle catch you remembering? Day eight.

At the wedding, there's a head table. At the restaurant, the best booth goes to the regulars. At the office party, the bosses somehow end up together. Where you sit tells everyone who you are. And then there's a hall where that's impossible. There are no chairs. Everyone sits on the floor, cross-legged, in long straight rows. A millionaire next to a laborer. A visitor who's never been inside next to a grandmother who's come every day for sixty years. The same volunteer walks down the row and puts the same food on every plate. Day one gave you the word for the hands doing that work. Today, the word for the meal itself.
screen: `WHERE YOU SIT SAYS WHO YOU ARE.` → `NO CHAIRS. LONG ROWS.` → `THE SAME FOOD ON EVERY PLATE.`

segments.voice: Langar. The word means the community kitchen, and the free meal that comes out of it. Gurdwaras keep one. Tradition traces the practice to Guru Nanak himself, who, in the town he founded at Kartarpur, shared food with everyone who came, and the Gurus after him built it into an institution. To see why it mattered, look at the world it was born into. In Nanak's Punjab, who you ate with was a serious matter. Rules of caste decided who could share food, who could touch whose plate, who could even cook for whom. Eating together across those lines could be a scandal. The langar did it on purpose, every day. The Gurus asked everyone who came to eat first, sitting side by side in rows, before anything else. That row even has its own name: pangat. Three details make the idea work. First, the floor. Nobody sits higher, because there's nothing to sit higher on. Some gurdwaras outside India have used tables, and communities have had real debates about that, but the floor is still the picture. Second, the food. Langar is simple and vegetarian, so that someone of any faith or any diet can eat it without worry. Nobody has to ask what's in it. Third, the guest list. There isn't one. Anyone. Any faith, or none. You don't have to be a Sikh, or explain why you're hungry, or say thank you in the right words. You sit down, you hold out your hands, and someone puts bread in them. The meal is a teaching you can taste: if there is one God, as we said on day four, then there is one row.

segments.voice: Sit on the floor if you can, or just let your weight settle wherever you are. Picture yourself in a long row in a langar hall. On your left, someone you'd never usually sit beside. On your right, someone else you'd never choose. Just sit with them in your mind. Nobody higher. Nobody lower. Hands open, waiting for the same bread. The bell holds the time.
Langar. The free community kitchen, and the meal where everyone sits on the floor, in one row, and eats the same food. Eighth word.
Your line: sit on the floor with a stranger. Today, at lunch or on a break, sit next to someone you usually wouldn't, and share something, even just the table. Day eight.

9.title: honest work
9.hook: honest work; Nanak's three pillars start here
9.howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to live as householders and to earn their living honestly through their own work, and kirat karni is named with sharing and remembering the name as one of the three pillars of Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: langar, the meal where everyone sits on the floor in one row. Your line was sit on the floor with a stranger. Who did you end up next to? Day nine.

A mountaintop. A begging bowl. A cave. Those are the classic pictures of a holy man: someone who has given away everything and lives on what people put in his bowl, or left his family behind to meditate alone. Seekers like that have been honored in many lands. Guru Nanak, back from his years on the road, after sitting with the teachers of his time, chose differently. He spent the rest of his life on a farm, in a village by a river, plowing fields, raising a family, growing food. The founder of a faith with his hands in the dirt. Today, the first of three pillars Sikhs build a life on.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINTOP. THE BEGGING BOWL. THE CAVE.` → `NANAK CHOOSES A FARM.` → `THE FIRST OF THREE PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Kirat karni. Kirat means honest labor, the work of your hands and your head. Karni means to do. So: do honest work. Earn your living, and earn it cleanly. Sikhs often describe the whole of daily life as resting on three pillars. This is the first. Tomorrow and the day after, the other two. Here's why this one mattered so much. In Nanak's day, there were seekers who left ordinary life behind: giving up work, family and home, and living on alms. Nanak honored sincere seekers wherever he met them, and he sat with them and talked with them. But the life he taught was the householder's life. You don't have to leave the world to find God. You find God in the middle of it, in the field, in the shop, at the kitchen table. So in the last years of his life, in the town of Kartarpur, the Guru farmed. And there's a line in the scripture, attributed to Guru Nanak, that Sikhs often quote to sum this up. In paraphrase: the one who eats what they've earned by their own effort, and gives some of it away with their own hand, that person recognizes the path. Notice the word honest. Kirat karni isn't just keep busy. It's work without cheating, without exploiting anyone, without taking what isn't yours. A small honest wage, the tradition says, is sweeter than a fortune earned crooked. You'll meet a famous story about exactly that later on the path, about a carpenter's plain bread. For now: the first pillar isn't in a temple. It's on Monday morning.
screen: `KIRAT — HONEST LABOR. KARNI — TO DO.` · `NOT LEAVING THE WORLD. LIVING IN IT.` · `THE GURU WHO FARMED.` · `EARNED BY EFFORT, WITHOUT CHEATING.` · then, large: `THE FIRST PILLAR IS MONDAY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Settle, and look at your hands for a moment. Think about the work they do: paid work, housework, schoolwork, caring for someone. Pick one piece of it you'll do today. Now picture doing it cleanly: no corner cut, no small lie, nothing taken that isn't yours. Just sit with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Kirat karni. Honest work: earning a living by your own effort, without cheating anyone. The first of three pillars. Ninth word.
Your line: earn it clean. Today, in one task, do the honest version even when a shortcut would go unnoticed. Day nine.

10.title: share what you earn
10.howItsDone: Sikhs practice vand chakna by sharing food, time and income with others; many give dasvandh, a tenth of their earnings, to the gurdwara, the langar or people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirat karni, honest work, the first pillar. Your line was earn it clean. Where did you skip the shortcut? Day ten.

Picture a kid with a bag of chips on the school bus. Their friend is looking at the bag. There's a tiny moment, you can almost see it, where the kid decides. Hold it tighter? Or tip the bag over and say, want some? Most of us made that decision a thousand times growing up, and we're still making it, just with bigger bags: a paycheck, a spare room, an afternoon. Yesterday was about how you earn. Earning honestly is only half of it, the Gurus said. The other half is what you do with the bag once it's in your hands. Today, the second pillar.
screen: `A BAG OF CHIPS ON THE BUS.` → `HOLD IT TIGHTER, OR TIP IT OVER?` → `THE SECOND PILLAR.`

segments.voice: Vand chakna. Vand means to share, to divide into portions. Chakna means to eat, to take your part. So: share, and then eat. Notice the order. Not eat, and share what's left over. Share first, then enjoy what's yours. Remember the line from the scripture from yesterday, the one who eats what they've earned by effort, and gives some away with their own hand. Yesterday was the first half. Today is the second: with their own hand. Not a tax, not a charity you've never seen. Your own hand, reaching out. Many Sikhs give in a particular way called dasvandh, which means a tenth. A tenth of what you earn, set aside for others and for the community: the langar, the gurdwara, someone in need. Some give exactly a tenth, some give what they can, and some give their time instead of money. It's practiced as a duty and a joy, not a fee to get in. And notice how the first two pillars lean on each other. Kirat karni alone could make you a hard worker who keeps everything. Vand chakna alone could make you generous with money you didn't earn fairly. Together they make a person who earns cleanly and then lets some of it go. The langar you met on day eight runs on exactly this: the flour, the lentils and the hands that cook them are given by the sangat. And what's shared isn't only money. Food on your plate, time on your calendar, attention, a skill you have: anything that came into your hands can go back out of them. Tomorrow, the third pillar, the one that holds these two up.
screen: `VAND — SHARE. CHAKNA — EAT.` · `SHARE FIRST, THEN ENJOY.` · `DASVANDH — A TENTH.` · `EARN CLEAN, THEN LET SOME GO.` · then, large: `WITH YOUR OWN HAND.`

segments.voice: Settle, and think about what came into your hands this week: money, food, time, a skill, a kindness. Pick one thing. Now picture dividing it, the way you'd tip the bag of chips over. Picture exactly who you'd hand a portion to, and their face when you do. Sit with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Vand chakna. Share, then eat: dividing what you've earned so others have a portion too. The second pillar. Tenth word.
Your line: the second pillar. Today, share one thing before you enjoy it: half a snack, an hour, a few dollars. Day ten.

11.title: the third
11.howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam japna by repeating Waheguru, reciting daily prayers and singing the scripture together in kirtan; with honest work and sharing it forms the three pillars of Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vand chakna, share, then eat. Your line was the second pillar. What did you share before you enjoyed it? Day eleven.

A stool with two legs will hold someone for a moment, if they're careful. Lean the wrong way and down they go. Add a third leg, and it holds all day. For two days we've been building something like that stool. Honest work. Sharing what you earn. Both good, both solid. But a person could do both and still run on empty: busy and generous and forgetting what any of it is for. In the Sikh telling, there's a third leg, and in a way it holds the other two up. Today, the last of the three pillars.
screen: `A STOOL WITH TWO LEGS.` → `BUSY, GENEROUS, AND EMPTY.` → `THE THIRD LEG.`

segments.voice: Naam japna. Naam, the name, the word you met on day five: not just a label but the whole presence of God, the truth running through everything. Japna means to repeat, to recite, to keep saying. So: keep the name. Remember God, again and again, all through the day. If this sounds familiar, it should. On day seven you learned simran, remembrance, Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath. Naam japna is the same heart, set in its place as a pillar of the whole life. It can be quiet, a word on the breath. It can be loud, a room full of people singing the scripture together to drums and harmonium. It can be reading, or listening, or simply catching yourself in the middle of a busy afternoon and remembering what's real. Here's how Sikh teachers explain why it sits with work and sharing. Without it, honest work can turn into pride: look how hard I work. Sharing can turn into a show: look how much I give. Remembering the name keeps both humble, because it reminds you where the strength to work and the things you share came from in the first place. And it runs the other way too. Remembering God without working honestly or sharing would float off into the clouds. The Sikh life keeps all three on the ground, together. Work with your hands. Share with your hands. Remember with your whole self. Earn it clean, share it first, and keep the name. That's the stool. Three legs, and a person can sit steady on it for a lifetime.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME. JAPNA — TO REPEAT.` · `SIMRAN, SET AS A PILLAR.` · `IT KEEPS WORK AND GIVING HUMBLE.` · `WORK, SHARE, REMEMBER, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE THREE PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and feel what you're sitting on, the chair, the floor, the bed. Notice how it holds you up without you thinking about it. Now breathe slowly. If you'd like, let the name ride on the breath: Wahe in, guru out. If that word isn't yours, let each breath carry one thing you want to remember is real. Just keep coming back to it. The bell holds the time.
Naam japna. Keeping the name: remembering God again and again, through the day. The third pillar, beside honest work and sharing. Eleventh word.
Your line: the three pillars. Today, see if you can touch all three before bed: one honest piece of work, one thing shared, one moment of remembering. Day eleven.

12.title: what it is and isn't
12.hook: what it is and isn't; a crown you tie yourself
12.howItsDone: Sikhs who wear a turban tie it fresh each morning to cover their uncut hair; men and some women wear them, and others cover their hair with a scarf. Everyone covers their head in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday: naam japna, keeping the name. Your line was the three pillars: work, share, remember. Did you touch all three? Day twelve.

Early morning, in homes all over the world, someone stands in front of a mirror with a long strip of cloth, several meters of it. They hold one end in their teeth, and wrap, and fold, and tuck, layer by layer, the same way they did yesterday and will tomorrow. Ten minutes, maybe less if they've been doing it for years. Plenty of people recognize the sight. Fewer know what it means. People have mistaken it for a costume, for a sign of some other faith, or for something to be afraid of. Today, what the Sikh turban is, and what it isn't.
screen: `A MIRROR, A LONG STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `WRAP, FOLD, TUCK.` → `RECOGNIZED, AND MISUNDERSTOOD.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi the turban is often called the dastar, a respectful word, or simply the pag. Start with what's underneath. Observant Sikhs keep their hair uncut, all their lives, as a way of accepting the body as it was made. The turban covers and protects that hair. So it isn't a hat you take on and off with the weather. It's part of a commitment. Now the history. Sikh tradition remembers that in the Gurus' time and place, a fine turban was a sign of rank, the headwear of kings and nobles. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, whom you'll meet properly in a few days, made the turban part of the identity of his community. The effect was deliberate: every Sikh, whoever their family was, wears a crown. Sikhs often describe it just like that. A crown you tie yourself, every morning. Some Sikh women wear one too; other Sikh women cover their hair with a scarf. And not every Sikh wears a turban. Some keep their hair and some don't, and Sikhs have real conversations about that. The scripture doesn't reduce faith to clothing. But for those who wear it, the turban does something else as well: it makes you visible. Sikhs sometimes say a Sikh should be easy to find in a crowd, so that anyone in trouble knows where to turn. You can't hide in a turban. And what it isn't: it isn't a sign of any other religion, it isn't a costume, and it isn't a threat. Sikhs have sometimes been mistaken and even targeted because of it, and some communities hold turban-tying days for their neighbors, to explain.
screen: `THE DASTAR COVERS UNCUT HAIR.` · `ONCE A SIGN OF KINGS.` · `EVERY SIKH WEARS A CROWN.` · `YOU CAN'T HIDE IN A TURBAN.` · then, large: `A CROWN YOU TIE YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Sit up, and let the crown of your head rise a little, as if something light and precious were resting there. Feel your spine lengthen underneath it. Breathe. Imagine walking into your day this way: not proud, just visible, steady, someone others could turn to if they needed help. Hold that posture. The bell holds the time.
The turban, the dastar. It covers uncut hair, marks a commitment, and makes every Sikh who wears it a crowned, visible person. Twelfth word.
Your line: carry yourself like it. Today, walk into one room as if you were wearing a crown: head up, steady, easy to find if someone needs you. Day twelve.

13.title: the congregation
13.hook: the congregation; why Sikhs never practice alone for long
13.howItsDone: Sikhs gather as a sangat in the gurdwara to sing kirtan, listen to the scripture, pray Ardas and eat langar together; many also meet in homes for readings and hymn-singing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the turban, a crown you tie yourself. Your line was carry yourself like it. Which room did you walk into with your head up? Day thirteen.

Around certain people, a person gets funnier, kinder, braver. Around others, more anxious, more cynical, quicker to gossip. Nobody gives an order. The room just does it. Parents know this; it's why they want to meet their kids' friends. Coaches know it. Anyone who has tried to quit something while their whole crowd kept doing it knows it. People become, a little at a time, like the people they sit with. The Gurus built that plain fact into the center of Sikh life. Today, the word for the company you keep.
screen: `FUNNIER AROUND SOME PEOPLE.` → `ANXIOUS AROUND OTHERS.` → `WE BECOME OUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Sangat. The congregation. The community gathered together, the company you keep. You'll often hear it as sadh sangat, the company of the holy, or satsangat, the true company. Everywhere Guru Nanak traveled, the stories say, he left a sangat behind: a small group of people who met to sing the hymns, share food and look after one another. Long before there were grand buildings, there were these circles of ordinary people. So what makes a sangat true? The scripture asks that very question. In paraphrase, the answer comes back simple: the true congregation is where the one name is spoken. Not where the building is finest or the people are richest. Where people gather around the name. Sikhs speak about the sangat with a startling kind of respect. There's a long tradition that the Guru is present wherever the sangat gathers, and that the voice of the congregation, deciding together, carries real weight. That's why so much of Sikh life happens with others: singing together, eating in one row together, doing seva together, bowing before the scripture together. Not because solitude is bad. Simran on your own breath matters. But the Gurus seem to have known that a person alone will drift, and a person in good company will be carried, the way a small boat is carried by a current. And here's the practical wisdom inside it. You can't always choose your family or your coworkers. But you can choose, at least some of the time, whose company you seek out. The tradition says: choose people who make you remember what's real.
screen: `SANGAT — THE COMPANY YOU KEEP.` · `NANAK LEFT A CIRCLE BEHIND.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `A PERSON ALONE DRIFTS.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY CARRIES YOU.`

Picture one of them clearly. Let yourself feel grateful for them, and let that gratitude sit for a while. The bell holds the time.
Sangat. The congregation, the company you keep. The circle gathered around the one name. Thirteenth word.
Your line: good company. Today, reach out to one person who brings out the best in you, and tell them so. Day thirteen.

14.title: the door of the guru
14.hook: the door of the guru; why it's open to anyone
14.carry: cover your head, take off your shoes, come in
14.howItsDone: Anyone may visit a gurdwara: visitors cover their heads, remove their shoes and wash their hands, sit on the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib for kirtan, receive karah prashad, and eat in the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangat, the company you keep. Your line was good company. Who did you tell? Day fourteen, the end of week two.

You're walking down a street you know, and you notice a tall triangular flag, saffron or deep blue, flying on a pole outside a building you never paid much attention to. Maybe it's a grand white building with domes. Maybe it's a converted warehouse, or an old church, or a house. Through the door you can hear singing, and drums, and smell something cooking. You might wonder: can I just walk in? Am I allowed? Do I have to be one of them? This week you've learned the kitchen, the pillars, the turban and the company. Today, the place where they all meet, and the answer to that question.

segments.voice: Gurdwara. Gur, the Guru. Dwara, a door, a gateway. The door of the Guru. It's the Sikh place of worship, and the flag outside, the Nishan Sahib, is there so it can be found from far away. And the answer to the question is yes. Anyone can walk in, of any faith or none. In Amritsar, the Golden Temple was built with doors on all four sides, which Sikhs explain as a welcome to people from every direction and every walk of life. There are just a few simple things everyone does, Sikh or not. Cover your head, with a scarf or a cloth, and gurdwaras usually keep some at the door. Take off your shoes. Wash your hands. Leave tobacco and alcohol outside. That's all. Inside, you'll find the week's words gathered in one place. At the front, on a raised platform under a canopy, rests the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib. People come in, bow before it, and sit on the floor, all at the same level. That's the sangat. Musicians sing hymns from the scripture: that's naam japna, out loud. Near the end, everyone may be offered karah prashad, a warm sweet made of flour, butter and sugar, placed in cupped hands, the same for everyone. Then, down the hall, the langar: the one row, the same meal. And the people cooking it, cleaning the floors, minding the shoes? That's seva, and every coin that keeps the lights on is someone's vand chakna. A gurdwara isn't only a place to pray. It's the whole path, given a building and a door that stays open.
screen: `GUR, THE GURU. DWARA, A DOOR.` · `OPEN TO ANYONE, FROM EVERY SIDE.` · `HEAD COVERED, SHOES OFF, HANDS WASHED.` · `THE WHOLE WEEK UNDER ONE ROOF.` · then, large: `A DOOR THAT STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Do the threshold with your body. Lift your hands to your head, as if laying a cloth over it. Rub your palms together slowly, as if rinsing them in cool water. Feel your feet on the floor, bare or as if they were. Then stay at the door: singing somewhere inside, the smell of the kitchen, and nobody asking who you are. Just stand at the threshold and listen. The bell holds the time.
The gurdwara. The door of the Guru, the Sikh place of worship, open to anyone. Fourteenth word. Two weeks.

Your line: cover your head, take off your shoes, come in. Look up the nearest gurdwara to you today, just to know it's there. Next week, the last of camp one: spirit, story, prayer and the book itself. Day fourteen.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: gur (the Guru) + duara (door): the door of the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh temple.
what it means: the door of the Guru, where the scripture rests and the congregation, the kitchen and the service all meet, open to anyone.
what a scholar hears: early Sikh gathering places were called dharamsals. the name gurdwara, the Guru's door, took hold later, and the Nishan Sahib marks one from a distance.
